quests.instruction: Say “ten pounds” quickly, as if pricing something. What often happens to the /n/ of “ten”?
options: It stays a tongue-tip /n/, because it is the last sound of the word and so is fixed
It often shifts towards /m/, because the lips are getting ready for the /p/
It disappears completely before the /p/, so “ten” sounds like “te pounds”
quests.correctAnswer: It often shifts towards /m/, because the lips are getting ready for the /p/
quests.hint: Say “ten pounds” slowly, then fast. Notice what your lips do before the /p/ begins.
quests.explanation: In fast speech your mouth starts preparing for the next sound before it finishes the current one. The tongue tip would normally close for /n/, but the lips are already preparing for /p/, so “ten pounds” often sounds like “tem pounds”. This kind of change is called assimilation: a sound becomes more like its neighbour.
quests.phoneticRule: In assimilation, a word-final sound takes on a feature of the following sound (here, the place of articulation), so an alveolar /n/ before a bilabial /p/ is often pronounced as bilabial [m].

quests.instruction: Why does “lean back” often sound like “leem back” in casual speech?
options: The lips prepare for the /b/, so the nasal is made at the lips, not the tongue tip
The speaker adds an /m/ by mistake, because “back” is a very common word in English
The /b/ of “back” moves back onto “lean”, so the phrase is heard as “leemb ack”
quests.correctAnswer: The lips prepare for the /b/, so the nasal is made at the lips, not the tongue tip
quests.hint: Think about where in your mouth the /n/ is made compared with the /b/. Which articulator is about to move?
quests.explanation: /n/ is normally made with the tongue tip against the ridge behind the upper teeth, while /b/ is made with the lips. In fast speech the mouth moves ahead to the lips, so the nasal becomes [m]: “leem back”. The change happens because of the next sound, not because of a mistake.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar nasals assimilate in place to a following bilabial consonant: /n/ becomes [m] before /p/, /b/ and /m/, an anticipatory change typical of casual speech.

quests.instruction: You are running late and text, “I’m on my way.” Which version of “on my way” shows the change?
options: “on my way”, with a clear tongue-tip /n/ before the /m/
“ong my way”, with the nasal moved to the back of the mouth
“om my way”, with the nasal made at the lips before the /m/
quests.correctAnswer: “om my way”, with the nasal made at the lips before the /m/
quests.hint: Look at the first sound of “my”. Which part of the mouth makes it, and how might the nasal before it adapt?
quests.explanation: /m/ is made with the lips, so the /n/ of “on” can shift to the lips: “om my way”. The two nasals then blend into one slightly longer /m/. It is a very common phrase in messages and phone calls.
quests.phoneticRule: When the changed sound and the following sound become the same consonant, the boundary can sound like a single lengthened consonant.

quests.instruction: You ask a friend, “Have you seen Mary?” Which version of “seen Mary” shows the change often heard in casual speech?
options: “seem Mary”, with the nasal made at the lips
“seen Mary”, with a clear tongue-tip /n/
“seeng Mary”, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
quests.correctAnswer: “seem Mary”, with the nasal made at the lips
quests.hint: Say “seen Mary” quickly and notice which part of your mouth is ready for the /m/ while the nasal is still sounding.
quests.explanation: The /m/ starts with the lips closing, so in quick speech the nasal before it is often made at the lips too: “seem Mary”. The vowel stays the same and only the nasal changes. Recognising this stops you from hearing an unfamiliar word instead of “seen”.
quests.phoneticRule: The change targets the word-final nasal only; the vowel before it and the consonant after it keep their normal quality.

quests.instruction: In “join me”, which sound changes, and which sound causes the change?
options: The /m/ of “me” changes into /n/ because of the /n/ of “join”
The vowel of “join” changes because of the /m/
The /n/ of “join” changes to /m/ because of the /m/ of “me”
quests.correctAnswer: The /n/ of “join” changes to /m/ because of the /m/ of “me”
quests.hint: Ask which sound comes first in time. The change usually happens to that earlier sound.
quests.explanation: The change works backwards in time: the earlier sound adapts to the later one. So the /n/ at the end of “join” becomes [m] before the /m/ of “me”: “joym me”. The /m/ of “me” stays as it is. Knowing the direction makes it easier to predict where changes occur.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation of place is typically regressive: the word-final alveolar takes the place of articulation of the following consonant, and the following consonant remains unchanged.

quests.instruction: You ask a colleague, “Do you have a plan B?” Which version of “plan B” shows the change?
options: “plang B”, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
“plan B”, with the tongue-tip /n/ kept clear
“plam B”, with the nasal made at the lips, not the tip
quests.correctAnswer: “plam B”, with the nasal made at the lips, not the tip
quests.hint: The letter B stands for a /b/ sound. Decide which place in the mouth makes it, then adapt the nasal.
quests.explanation: The /b/ in “B” is made with the lips, so the /n/ of “plan” often shifts to [m]: “plam B”. It works with a single letter name just as with a full word, because only the following sound matters.
quests.phoneticRule: The trigger can be any word beginning with a bilabial, including single-letter names such as B or P; what matters is the sound, not the word type.

quests.instruction: Say “phone call” at conversation speed. What often happens to the /n/ at the end of “phone”?
options: It becomes /m/, because the lips start to get ready for the beginning of “call”
It often becomes [ŋ], the “ng” sound, as the tongue moves back in readiness for the /k/
It stays exactly the same, because a word-final sound is fixed in place and cannot change
quests.correctAnswer: It often becomes [ŋ], the “ng” sound, as the tongue moves back in readiness for the /k/
quests.hint: Say “phone call” slowly, then quickly. Notice where the back of your tongue is heading for the /k/.
quests.explanation: /k/ is made at the back of the mouth, where the back of the tongue touches the soft palate. In quick speech the tongue can move there early, so the /n/ becomes [ŋ], the “ng” sound: “fohng call”. The words are still “phone call”; only the position of the nasal has changed.
quests.phoneticRule: Before a velar stop (/k/ or /g/), an alveolar /n/ is commonly realised as velar [ŋ] in casual speech.

quests.instruction: Choose the explanation that fits “green card” sounding like “greeng card”.
options: A letter “g” is added in speech because “card” begins with a hard “c” sound
The tongue moves back for /k/, so the nasal shifts to [ŋ] a little early
The /k/ of “card” moves back onto “green”, so the phrase is heard as “greenk ard”
quests.correctAnswer: The tongue moves back for /k/, so the nasal shifts to [ŋ] a little early
quests.hint: Say “ing”, then say “green” before a /k/, and compare where your tongue is at the end of the nasal.
quests.explanation: No letter is added; the “ng” sound is [ŋ], made with the back of the tongue raised. Because /k/ needs that same tongue position, the nasal in “green” often shifts there early. The spelling stays “green card”, but the sound is closer to “greeng card”.
quests.phoneticRule: The change is phonetic, not orthographic: the nasal takes the velar place of the following /k/ or /g/ without any change to the spelling or the identity of the words.

quests.instruction: Which version of “one game” shows the change often heard before a /g/?
options: “wung game”, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
“wum game”, with the nasal made at the lips before the /g/
“wun game”, with the tongue-tip closure kept clear and unchanged
quests.correctAnswer: “wung game”, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
quests.hint: Compare the first sound of “game” with the /k/ from the earlier examples. Which place in the mouth do they share?
quests.explanation: /g/ is made at the back of the mouth, like /k/, so the /n/ of “one” often shifts to [ŋ] before it: “wung game”. It is the same pattern as “phone call”; only the following consonant differs.
quests.phoneticRule: Both velar stops, /k/ and /g/, trigger the same shift of /n/ to [ŋ], because they share the same place of articulation.

quests.instruction: Predict which version of “that man” shows the change often heard in casual speech.
options: “thak man”, with the /t/ made at the back of the mouth
“that man”, with a clear tongue-tip /t/ released before the /m/
“thap man”, with the /t/ made at the lips before the /m/
quests.correctAnswer: “thap man”, with the /t/ made at the lips before the /m/
quests.hint: Look at the first sound of “man” and decide where in the mouth it is made, then ask which sound before it could copy that place.
quests.explanation: /m/ is made with the lips, so the /t/ before it can move to the lips as well: [p]. The result sounds like “thap man”. The /t/ stays voiceless and still stops the airflow; only its place changes. Some speakers use a brief throat stop for /t/ instead, and the lip closure of the following sound is what you hear then.
quests.phoneticRule: Before a bilabial consonant, the alveolar stop /t/ can be realised as bilabial [p], keeping its voicelessness and stop quality.

quests.instruction: In “great party”, what happens to the /t/ when the phrase is said quickly and casually?
options: It can become a /p/ sound, made at the lips, before the /p/ of “party”
It can become a /k/ sound, made at the back of the mouth, before the /p/ of “party”
It becomes a /d/, because the next word’s vowel is voiced
quests.correctAnswer: It can become a /p/ sound, made at the lips, before the /p/ of “party”
quests.hint: Notice that “party” begins with a lip sound, and think about what your tongue tip does when the lips are about to close.
quests.explanation: The /p/ of “party” is made with the lips, so the /t/ before it can move to the lips. Because both sounds are then identical, they merge into one longer /p/: “grayp party”. Recognising this prevents you from searching for a word like “grape”.
quests.phoneticRule: When the assimilated sound matches the following consonant exactly, the two can merge into a single lengthened consonant, which is why the boundary can seem to disappear.

quests.instruction: Apply the change to “meet Mum” in “Come and meet Mum.” Which version shows it?
options: “meek Mum”, with the /t/ made at the back of the mouth
“meep Mum”, with the /t/ made at the lips
“mee Mum”, with the /t/ left out entirely
quests.correctAnswer: “meep Mum”, with the /t/ made at the lips
quests.hint: Repeat “meet” before “Mum” and notice which sound your lips are about to make.
quests.explanation: The /m/ of “Mum” starts with lip closure, so the /t/ of “meet” often moves to the lips: “meep Mum”. It is the same pattern as “that man”; the following consonant is unaffected.
quests.phoneticRule: All three bilabial consonants (/p/, /b/ and /m/) trigger the shift equally, so the choice of trigger does not change the pattern.

quests.instruction: Which change is often heard in “red bus” in fast, casual speech?
options: The /d/ becomes /k/, made at the back of the mouth
The /b/ of “bus” becomes /d/ to match the /d/ of “red”
The /d/ becomes /b/, made at the lips, not the tongue
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ becomes /b/, made at the lips, not the tongue
quests.hint: Say “red bus” quickly and notice what your lips do before the /b/ starts.
quests.explanation: The /d/ at the end of “red” is made with the tongue tip, but /b/ starts with the lips. In casual speech the /d/ often shifts to the lips as [b], so it sounds like “reb bus”, with a slightly long /b/. The /b/ of “bus” is not affected.
quests.phoneticRule: The voiced alveolar stop /d/ can be realised as bilabial [b] before /p/, /b/ or /m/, keeping its voicing.

quests.instruction: Compare the change in “ten pounds” with the change in “bad back”. What do the two changes have in common?
options: Both involve a nasal consonant moving to the lips before a lip sound
Both involve a tongue-tip sound moving to the lips because a lip sound follows
Both involve the first sound of the second word changing to match the first word
quests.correctAnswer: Both involve a tongue-tip sound moving to the lips because a lip sound follows
quests.hint: Identify which sound changes in each phrase, and which sound causes the change.
quests.explanation: In both phrases, a tongue-tip consonant at the end of the first word (the /n/ of “ten” and the /d/ of “bad”) moves to the lips because the next word starts with a lip consonant. The trigger stays the same; only the affected sound differs. This is what makes the pattern predictable.
quests.phoneticRule: The pattern is general: the alveolar consonants /t/, /d/ and /n/ can take the place of a following bilabial, and the following consonant stays unchanged.

quests.instruction: Which version of “could be” shows the change in casual speech?
options: /kʊb bi/, with the /d/ made at the lips
/kʊd bi/, with a clear tongue-tip /d/
/kʊɡ bi/, with the /d/ made at the back of the mouth
quests.correctAnswer: /kʊb bi/, with the /d/ made at the lips
quests.hint: The word “be” starts with /b/. Decide which place in the mouth it shares with the changing sound.
quests.explanation: /b/ is a lip sound, so the /d/ of “could” can shift to the lips: /kʊb bi/. Because both are then /b/, the two merge into one slightly longer /b/. It is a common change in phrases such as “could be” and “would be”.
quests.phoneticRule: Modal verbs ending in /d/ (could, would, should) frequently show this change before bilabials, as in “could be” or “would pay”.

quests.instruction: You order “hot coffee” at a café. Which version shows the change often heard in casual speech?
options: “hok coffee”, with the /t/ made at the back of the mouth
“hop coffee”, with the /t/ made at the lips before the /k/
“hot coffee”, with the tongue-tip /t/ released clearly
quests.correctAnswer: “hok coffee”, with the /t/ made at the back of the mouth
quests.hint: The next word begins with a /k/; feel where the back of your tongue rises when you say it.
quests.explanation: /k/ is made at the back of the mouth, so the /t/ of “hot” can move there too: [k]. The two /k/ sounds then blend into one slightly longer /k/: “hok coffee”. This is a common everyday realisation when ordering drinks.
quests.phoneticRule: Before a velar stop, alveolar /t/ and /d/ can be realised as velar [k] and [g], sharing the place of the following consonant.

quests.instruction: In “bad cold”, which sound is changed by the /k/ that follows?
options: The /b/ at the start of “bad”
The /l/ in the middle of “cold”
The /d/ ending the word “bad”
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ ending the word “bad”
quests.hint: Only a sound at the edge of the first word can change here. Which sound is that?
quests.explanation: The /d/ closes “bad” and sits right before /k/, so it can adapt to the back-of-mouth place of /k/ and be heard as [g]: /bæɡ kəʊld/. The /b/ is too far away to be affected, and the /k/ in “cold” stays as it is.
quests.phoneticRule: Only the word-final alveolar consonant assimilates; consonants inside the word and the trigger consonant are not affected.

quests.instruction: You tell a friend, “I’m not going.” Which version of “not going” shows the change?
options: “nok going”, with the /t/ made at the back of the mouth
“nop going”, with the /t/ made at the lips
“nod going”, with the /t/ fully voiced into a /d/ before the /g/
quests.correctAnswer: “nok going”, with the /t/ made at the back of the mouth
quests.hint: Say “not going” in a hurry, then check which sound of “going” your tongue is preparing for.
quests.explanation: /g/ is a back-of-the-mouth sound, so the /t/ of “not” can shift to the back: [k]. The /t/ stays voiceless, so you typically hear /k/ rather than /g/, followed by the /g/ of “going”. It is very common with negatives such as “not going”.
quests.phoneticRule: Voiceless /t/ typically keeps its voicelessness when it takes velar place, so it is realised as [k] rather than [g] before /g/.

quests.instruction: A learner says “plan my day” with a clear /n/ every time. Another says “plam my day”. Which statement is fair?
options: The clear /n/ is wrong, because English requires the change whenever an /m/ follows
Both are acceptable: the change is common but optional, and depends on speed and style
The changed version is wrong, because the spelling has an “n” and speech should match the spelling
quests.correctAnswer: Both are acceptable: the change is common but optional, and depends on speed and style
quests.hint: Think about how the same speaker may say a phrase differently in careful and in casual situations.
quests.explanation: Assimilation is a tendency, not a rule that every speaker must apply. In careful or slow speech the /n/ may stay clear; in casual speech it often shifts to [m]. Both are normal, and the change can also be partial, with a sound somewhere between [n] and [m]. For listening, the aim is to recognise the change, not to expect it.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation is variable: it depends on speech rate, formality and the speaker, and the result can be partial (an intermediate articulation) rather than a complete change.

quests.instruction: A listener hears the /t/ in “that boy” as halfway between a /t/ and a /p/. What is happening?
options: The speaker is mispronouncing the word and should repeat it more slowly and carefully next time
The /t/ has been replaced by a full /p/ in every case, so the listener misheard it
The change is partial: the lips have begun to close, but the tongue tip is still involved
quests.correctAnswer: The change is partial: the lips have begun to close, but the tongue tip is still involved
quests.hint: Consider that the mouth moves gradually, not in sudden jumps.
quests.explanation: The tongue tip and the lips can overlap in time, so the /t/ may be only partly changed. What you hear can sit between [t] and [p], especially at moderate speed. This is normal variation, not an error.
quests.phoneticRule: Gradient assimilation involves overlapping articulatory gestures, so a listener may hear an intermediate sound rather than a clean category change.

quests.instruction: You say, “I would buy it.” Which version of “would buy” is a normal casual variant showing assimilation?
options: /wʊt baɪ/, with the /d/ devoiced into a /t/
/wʊb baɪ/, with the /d/ made at the lips instead
/wʊɡ baɪ/, with the /d/ made at the back of the mouth
quests.correctAnswer: /wʊb baɪ/, with the /d/ made at the lips instead
quests.hint: Ask which sound in the phrase asks for lip closure, and whether the /d/ could move to that place.
quests.explanation: The /b/ of “buy” involves lip closure, so the /d/ of “would” can shift to the lips and merge with it: /wʊb baɪ/. It is a common casual variant, not a required form. A clear /d/ is still perfectly acceptable, especially in careful speech.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilated forms are optional variants: both the assimilated and the citation form are acceptable, and the choice reflects style rather than correctness.

quests.instruction: In casual speech “green paint” often sounds like “greem paint”. Which sound causes the change without changing itself?
options: The /p/ at the very start of “paint”
The long vowel /iː/ inside the word “green”
The /n/ at the very end of the word “green”
quests.correctAnswer: The /p/ at the very start of “paint”
quests.hint: The changing sound adapts to a neighbour. Ask which neighbour is doing the pulling.
quests.explanation: In assimilation, the earlier sound adapts to the later one. The /p/ at the start of “paint” is the trigger, and it stays as it is, while the /n/ at the end of “green” moves to the lips. So the word that follows is not changed by the word before it.
quests.phoneticRule: The trigger of assimilation is unchanged; only the earlier, word-final alveolar shifts its place of articulation.

quests.instruction: In “this bag”, does the /s/ take the lip place of the /b/, the way /n/ does in “ten pounds”?
options: Yes: it becomes /f/, because /f/ is the lip sound closest to an /s/ in English
No: /s/ usually keeps its place before a lip sound, so the /s/ stays clear
Yes: it becomes /b/ and merges with the /b/ at the start of “bag”
quests.correctAnswer: No: /s/ usually keeps its place before a lip sound, so the /s/ stays clear
quests.hint: Recall which consonants were involved in every example so far: /n/, /t/ and /d/. Is /s/ one of them?
quests.explanation: The place shift you have studied mainly affects /t/, /d/ and /n/ at the end of a word. The /s/ in “this” does not usually move to the lips before /b/. Applying the pattern to every consonant would lead you to expect changes that do not typically happen.
quests.phoneticRule: Place assimilation of this kind is characteristic of the alveolar stops and nasal (/t/, /d/, /n/); other alveolars such as /s/ and /z/ are not usually affected by bilabial or velar neighbours in the same way.

quests.instruction: You ask a friend, “Have you seen Dan?” What happens to the /n/ of “seen” before the /d/ of “Dan”?
options: It becomes /m/, made at the lips, to match the first sound of “Dan”
It becomes [ŋ], made at the back of the mouth, to match the first sound of “Dan”
It stays a tongue-tip /n/, because /d/ is made at the same place as /n/
quests.correctAnswer: It stays a tongue-tip /n/, because /d/ is made at the same place as /n/
quests.hint: Compare where /n/ and /d/ are made in the mouth.
quests.explanation: /n/ and /d/ are both made with the tongue tip touching the ridge behind the upper teeth. There is no difference in place for the /n/ to adopt, so “seen Dan” keeps its tongue-tip /n/. Assimilation needs a difference in place between the two neighbouring sounds.
quests.phoneticRule: Place assimilation requires a mismatch in place: an alveolar followed by another alveolar has no place change to make.

quests.instruction: Which word boundary in “Please turn back at the bridge” shows assimilation?
quests.word: Please turn back at the bridge
quests.textToSpeak: Please turn back at the bridge
options: “Please turn”, where the /z/ changes its place to match /t/
“back at”, where the /k/ links to the vowel of “at”
“turn back”, where the /n/ moves to the lips before /b/
quests.correctAnswer: “turn back”, where the /n/ moves to the lips before /b/
quests.hint: Check each boundary and ask whether a consonant changes its place or simply moves to the next word.
quests.explanation: At “turn back” the /n/ can shift to [m] because /b/ follows: “turm back”. The boundary “back at” is linking, not assimilation, because the /k/ stays a /k/ and simply joins “at”. Telling the two apart shows whether a sound has changed or only moved.
quests.phoneticRule: In a sentence, assimilation is identified by a changed articulation of a word-final consonant, whereas linking only relocates an unchanged consonant to the next syllable.
quests.spokenForm: Please turm back at the bridge

quests.instruction: In a shop you say, “Take that bag upstairs.” Which spoken version of “that bag” shows the change?
options: “thap bag”, with the /t/ made at the lips before the /b/
“thak bag”, with the /t/ made at the back of the mouth
“that bag”, with a fully released tongue-tip /t/ and a small pause
quests.correctAnswer: “thap bag”, with the /t/ made at the lips before the /b/
quests.hint: The word after “that” starts with a lip sound; think about which place the /t/ might borrow.
quests.explanation: The /b/ of “bag” is made with the lips, so the /t/ of “that” can shift to the lips: “thap bag”. The rest of the sentence is unaffected, which is why you can spot the change by looking only at the boundary that involves a tongue-tip consonant before a lip or back sound.
quests.phoneticRule: In a full sentence, the assimilation site is found by scanning for word-final /t/, /d/ or /n/ followed by a bilabial or velar consonant.

quests.instruction: In “We should be at home”, one boundary shows assimilation and another shows a glide link. Which pair is correct?
options: Assimilation at “be at”, and a glide at “should be”
Assimilation at “should be”, and a glide at “be at”
Assimilation at “at home”, and a glide at “We should”
quests.correctAnswer: Assimilation at “should be”, and a glide at “be at”
quests.hint: One boundary has a tongue-tip consonant before a lip sound. Another has a vowel before a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Should be” has a /d/ before /b/, so the /d/ can shift to the lips. “Be at” has a vowel followed by a vowel, so a light /j/ glide appears. So the same short sentence can contain a changed sound and an inserted glide, and each has a different cause.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation and glide insertion are triggered by different boundary types: a consonant before a consonant of a different place, versus a vowel before a vowel.

quests.instruction: In “gone missing”, the /n/ often sounds like an /m/. Which description of the change is correct?
options: The /m/ of “missing” changes because of the /n/ of “gone” before it
The /n/ of “gone” changes because of the /m/ of “missing” that follows
The /g/ of “gone” changes because of the /n/ that comes straight after it
quests.correctAnswer: The /n/ of “gone” changes because of the /m/ of “missing” that follows
quests.hint: Ask which sound comes first, and which one is doing the influencing.
quests.explanation: The final /n/ of “gone” shifts to [m] under the influence of the /m/ that starts “missing”: “gom missing”. The influence runs backwards: the following sound is the trigger and the preceding sound is the one that changes.
quests.phoneticRule: In place assimilation the triggering consonant is the later sound and the changing consonant is the earlier word-final alveolar (regressive assimilation).

quests.instruction: You are packing for a holiday. Predict which version of “sun cream” shows assimilation.
options: “sum cream”, with the nasal made at the lips
“sun cream”, with the /n/ made with the tongue tip as usual
“sung cream”, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
quests.correctAnswer: “sung cream”, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
quests.hint: Identify the place in the mouth of the /k/ that follows, then match the nasal to it.
quests.explanation: /k/ is made at the back of the mouth, so the /n/ of “sun” can shift to [ŋ]: “sung cream”. Using the place of the trigger, you can predict this without having heard it. The word is still “sun”; only its final sound has moved.
quests.phoneticRule: Predicting assimilation is a two-step check: find the place of articulation of the following consonant, then match the word-final alveolar to it (lips for /p b m/, back of the mouth for /k g/).

quests.instruction: Compare “ten apples” with “ten pounds”. What is the key difference between the two?
options: In “ten apples” the /n/ stays an /n/ and moves on; in “ten pounds” the /n/ itself changes
Both are linking, because both first words end in /n/ and another sound follows
Both are assimilation, because a consonant or a vowel follows the /n/ in both
quests.correctAnswer: In “ten apples” the /n/ stays an /n/ and moves on; in “ten pounds” the /n/ itself changes
quests.hint: Ask whether the /n/ keeps its identity or takes on a new place of articulation in each phrase.
quests.explanation: In “ten apples”, a vowel follows, so the /n/ simply moves onto “apples” and is still an /n/: this is linking. In “ten pounds”, a lip consonant follows, so the /n/ itself changes place to [m]: this is assimilation. Telling these apart shows whether a sound has moved or changed.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking changes only which syllable a consonant belongs to, whereas assimilation changes the consonant's own articulation (its place or voicing).
